passage:
Irfan, you asked your Sarika Aunty how my family handled my father-in-law's old age. Let me tell you, we nearly got it wrong. After his fall, my husband and his brothers sat in the drawing room discussing whether to move him to a flat near us. He was sitting right there, and nobody asked him anything.
I said, "Abba, what do you want?" The room went quiet. He said, "I want to stay in my own house, near my mosque, with my plants."
So we planned around that. Grab rails in the bathroom, his bed moved downstairs. My husband took the doctor visits, one brother took the weekly shopping, and my sister-in-law and I shared the evening calls. It wasn't perfect. Some weeks we argued. But he lived there happily for six more years, and he always said we listened.

qa.q: Where did Abba want to stay?
qa.a: He wanted to stay in his own house, near his mosque, with his plants.

qa.q: How do you think Abba felt when Sarika asked him what he wanted?
qa.a: He probably felt respected and relieved to be included after being talked about as if he weren't there.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the family's planning, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Sarika asking Abba directly, because then the family planned around his wishes and shared the jobs fairly.

qa.q: How might the brothers have felt when the room went quiet?
qa.a: They were probably surprised and a little ashamed, realising they had been deciding for Abba without asking him.

grounding: It shows a family learning to talk with an ageing parent instead of over him, adapting his home for safety and sharing tasks among siblings and in-laws.

The video call kept freezing. Wasim's sister in Dubai had one hour before her flight, the village network was patchy, and Ammi was sitting between Wasim and his wife, Keerthana, on the charpai, squinting at the phone.
"Let's be quick," said his sister. "Ammi should move to the city with Wasim."
Keerthana gently turned the phone. "Before we decide, can we ask Ammi?"
Ammi looked surprised. "I want to stay here. But the bathroom floor frightens me at night."
"Then we fix the floor," Wasim said. "Non-slip tiles and a light."
"I'll pay for the tiles," said his sister, her face pixelating.
"I'll come on weekends," said Keerthana. "Wasim does weekdays by phone, and the neighbour's son checks in each evening."
The call dropped. Ammi patted Keerthana's hand. "You asked me first," she said.

qa.q: What frightens Ammi at night?
qa.a: The bathroom floor frightens her at night.

qa.q: How did Ammi feel when Keerthana asked her first?
qa.a: Ammi felt surprised and then grateful and respected, which shows when she patted Keerthana's hand.

qa.q: Which choice made this family plan work, even with the bad network?
qa.a: Stopping to ask Ammi what she wanted, then fixing the real safety worry and splitting the tasks among everyone.

qa.q: How might Wasim's sister see the plan after the call dropped?
qa.a: She might feel relieved to have a clear part, paying for the tiles, even from far away and in a rush.

grounding: It shows a family talking with an ageing mother rather than over her, making the home safer and dividing tasks fairly among siblings and in-laws.

passage: After their mother's second fall, Himani, twenty-six, called a family meeting in the Lucknow house. Her brothers came, and so did her sister-in-law. At first they all talked across the table as if Minakshi weren't there. 'She should move in with one of us.' 'She needs a full-time helper.' Himani stopped them. 'Amma is sitting right here. Amma, what do you want?' Minakshi, seventy, looked surprised. 'I want to stay in my own house. But I'm scared of the bathroom.' So they started there. Grab rails in the bathroom, a night light in the corridor, a phone by her bed. Himani's elder brother would handle the doctor visits, the younger one the groceries, and their sister-in-law would visit on Wednesdays. It wasn't perfect. But Minakshi said, 'Thank you for asking me.'

qa.q: What did the family put in the bathroom?
qa.a: Grab rails.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when the others talked across the table?
qa.a: Himani felt frustrated and protective, seeing Amma treated as if she were not there.

qa.q: What did Himani do that made the planning respectful?
qa.a: She stopped them talking over their mother and asked Minakshi what she wanted, then shared tasks fairly.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when her children talked across the table?
qa.a: She probably felt invisible and hurt, as if decisions about her life did not include her.

'Sarita Ma, we want to talk about the house. But only with you, not about you.'
Sarita looked around the table at her daughters and son-in-law. 'That's new.'
Minakshi smiled. 'We deserve that. What would you like?'
'I want to keep my garden. And my Tuesday bhajan group.'
'Okay. What worries you?'
Sarita hesitated. 'The stairs to the bedroom. I nearly fell last week.' 
'Would you like your bedroom moved downstairs, near the garden?'
'Only if my bed goes with it.'
'Done.' Minakshi turned to the others. 'I'll handle the carpenter. Priya does doctor visits. Rahul drives to bhajans.'
'And who does Sundays?' asked Sarita.
'We rotate,' said Minakshi. 'And we check with you if anything changes.'
Sarita reached for her daughter's hand. 'I feel listened to. That's enough for today.'

qa.q: What did Sarita want to keep?
qa.a: Her garden and her Tuesday bhajan group.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel at the end of the talk?
qa.a: She felt listened to and relieved, reaching for her daughter's hand.

qa.q: What made this family conversation work?
qa.a: They talked with Sarita, asked what she wanted and worried about, adapted the house and divided the tasks fairly.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when Sarita said 'That's new'?
qa.a: She probably felt a little embarrassed but determined to do things better this time.

grounding: Shows a family planning with an ageing parent rather than over her, adapting the home for safety and sharing responsibilities fairly.

subtopic: Ageing parents' physical changes and how family responds
passage: When Appa's eyesight started failing last year, my brother Joseph and I made every mistake at first. We argued about him on the phone as if he couldn't hear. We rearranged his kitchen without asking, and he couldn't find his own tea. He went quiet for a week. I'm Gopika, and that silence taught me. We sat down with him on the veranda and asked, 'Appa, what's hardest? What do you want to keep doing?' He said he wanted to keep walking to church and cooking his Sunday fish curry. So we put bright tape on the steps, labelled his spice jars in big letters and got a talking clock. Joseph took the hospital visits, I took the groceries, and his neighbour walks with him on Sundays. He still grumbles. But he's in charge of his own life again.

qa.q: What did Gopika and Joseph put on the steps?
qa.a: Bright tape.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel after Appa went quiet for a week?
qa.a: Gopika felt guilty and sobered, realising they had been making decisions over him.

qa.q: What changed once they asked Appa what he wanted?
qa.a: They adapted the home to keep him independent and shared responsibilities fairly between the siblings and a neighbour.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt when he couldn't find his own tea?
qa.a: He probably felt frustrated and hurt, as if his own kitchen was no longer his.

grounding: Shows a family learning to plan with an ageing parent rather than over him, adapting the home and dividing responsibilities with consistent kindness.

Home visit note, Sethi family, Saturday.
I came to discuss safety after Mr Sethi's fall. Before I could open my file, his daughter Simran pulled a chair to his side and said, "Papa, what do you want this to look like?" He wanted to keep his room upstairs. We talked it through with him, not around him: a rail on the staircase, a night lamp, the pressure cooker moved to a lower shelf. Simran had a list for the siblings too: her brother takes the doctor visits, her sister-in-law does the groceries on Wednesdays, Simran does Sundays. Mr Sethi grumbled that he was "being managed", then asked for a bell by his bed himself. Nobody had every answer. But the tone stayed kind all the way through. I'll check the rail next week.
Devika, community nurse

qa.q: What did Mr Sethi ask for himself?
qa.a: A bell by his bed.

qa.q: Why did Mr Sethi grumble that he was being managed?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a little proud, worried about losing control, yet being asked first let him join in.

qa.q: What did Simran's family get right in this meeting?
qa.a: They asked Mr Sethi what he wanted first, adapted the home around his choices, and divided tasks fairly among siblings and in-laws.

qa.q: How does the nurse see the family's planning?
qa.a: The nurse sees that not every answer was found, but values the kind, steady tone and plans to follow up on the rail.

grounding: Shows a family talking with an ageing parent rather than over him, adapting the home for safety and sharing tasks fairly among siblings and in-laws.
